02

What it costs
to leave it

Three consequences, all of them things you are already paying for whether or not the line item exists.

You compete on price

When the buyer can’t tell the difference between you and the next quote, the only remaining variable is the number at the bottom.

Every project restarts the argument

Without a written position, each new campaign relitigates what the company is. That is expensive, and it is paid in your time.

Good work gets rejected for the wrong reason

Teams reject work that feels wrong when what they mean is the strategy was never agreed. The design takes the blame.

04

How we work it

Four steps, with the real deliverable named at each one. If a step does not produce something you can hold, it is not a step.

Step 01

Excavate

Interviews with your team, your best clients and — where it is useful — the ones who chose someone else.

Deliverable — Findings memo

Step 02

Name the problem

The real one, in the market’s language rather than yours. This is usually the uncomfortable part.

Deliverable — Positioning statement

Step 03

Frame the category

Where you sit, what you are compared against, and what you deliberately are not.

Deliverable — Category map + competitive frame

Step 04

Write the language

The words your team uses on calls, on the site and in the deck. One vocabulary, everywhere.

Deliverable — Messaging framework

07

The objections you were about to raise

Possibly. The test is whether five people on your team describe it the same way without checking with each other. If they do, you don’t need this and we’ll say so on the call.

Strategy work is measured in weeks, not months, and the deliverable is a document short enough that people actually read it. We’ll scope the specific timeline once we know how many stakeholders have a veto.

Usually because it ended at a document. Ours ends at applied language — the site, the deck, the sales call — because a position nobody uses is just a nicer way to describe the same problem.
